summary: Mathematical precision for ages 8-9: tie units to what is measured (area counts unit squares, so it is cm², not a bare number or a length unit), keep 24-hour time distinct from 12-hour am/pm (15:45 is the same moment as 3:45 pm, but '15:45 pm' is a contradiction), name angle types against a right angle (acute smaller, obtuse larger and less than a straight angle), and treat 'three fourths' and 'three quarters' as two names for the same value. The teaching move throughout is to rephrase vague language into precise mathematical language and ask the child to say why the exact unit or notation matters, rather than only marking an answer wrong.
misconceptions: Gives an area with no unit or a length unit — '63' or '63 cm' instead of '63 cm²'
Mixes 24-hour and 12-hour notation — writes '15:45 pm', or cannot relate 15:45 to 3:45 pm
Names angle types imprecisely — swaps acute and obtuse, or says 'big angle'
Treats 'three fourths' and 'three quarters' as different amounts rather than two correct names for the same value

activities.title: Tiling to find the unit for area
steps: Enter or write the area of a rectangle, e.g. '63'.
Fill (or draw) the rectangle with unit squares that tile it exactly, counting the squares.
Revise the answer to carry a square unit: '63 cm²' or '63 square centimetres'.
Contrast an edge length of 63 cm (a length measured along one side) with an area of 63 cm² (unit squares covering the inside), and say why they are different quantities.
Answer the prompt: 'why does the unit have to be square?'
activities.insight: Area counts how many unit squares cover a region, so its unit is a square unit (cm²); a bare number says how many but not of what, and a plain length unit (cm) describes a distance, not a covering.

activities.title: One moment, two clocks: 24-hour vs am/pm
steps: Read a time written in 24-hour notation, e.g. 15:45.

Convert it to 12-hour am/pm: for times from 13:00 to 23:59, subtract 12 from the hour and write pm (15 − 12 = 3, giving 3:45 pm); 12:00–12:59 stays 12 and is pm, 00:00–00:59 becomes 12 am, and 01:00–11:59 keep their hour and are am. Check both show the same moment on a dual clock display.
Decide whether '15:45 pm' can be correct, and explain what the 'pm' clashes with.
Write the same time correctly in each system and state that 24-hour time runs 00:00–23:59 with no am/pm.
activities.insight: 24-hour and 12-hour are two complete, separate ways of naming the same moment; 'pm' belongs only to the 12-hour system, so stamping it onto a 24-hour time mixes two systems and contradicts itself.

activities.title: Naming angles against a right angle
steps: Place or overlay a right-angle template on a given angle.
Decide whether the angle is smaller than a right angle (acute), exactly a right angle (right angle), or larger than a right angle but less than a straight angle (obtuse).
State the angle type using the correct term and justify it by the comparison, avoiding 'big angle' or 'small angle'.
Repeat for several angles, including some close to a right angle.
activities.insight: Angle names are defined by comparison to a right angle (acute < right < obtuse), so the right angle is the reference that makes the vocabulary precise and reliable.

activities.title: Two names, one value: fraction vocabulary
steps: Match fraction words to symbols, e.g. 'three quarters' = 'three fourths' = ¾.
Explain that 'three fourths' and 'three quarters' name the same amount, not two different amounts.
Read notation aloud (=, <, >, ÷, ×) and state what each symbol means in a given statement.
activities.insight: A value can have more than one correct name; 'quarter' and 'fourth' are two words for the same part, and symbols carry fixed meanings that should be read and explained, not just copied.

activities.title: In-role questioner who takes answers literally
steps: Give answers to a character (e.g. a robot or timetable clerk) who queries anything imprecise: '63 what — is that a length or an area?', 'you can't put pm on a 24-hour time'.
Specify the missing unit or repair the mixed notation in response to each query.
State in your own words why the correction matters.
activities.insight: Precision is what lets another reader interpret an answer correctly; a bare number or mixed notation leaves the meaning ambiguous.

activities.title: Fix-the-notation screener
steps: Complete items that add the missing unit to an answer (e.g. turn '63' into '63 cm²').
Convert between 24-hour and am/pm (e.g. 15:45 ↔ 3:45 pm) and flag a mixed form like '15:45 pm' as wrong.
Identify a diagnostic case: 'A child wrote the area as 63 and a time as 15:45 pm — fix anything that isn't right and say why the missing or wrong part matters.'
activities.insight: Quick items can reveal who leaves units off or mixes time systems, pointing to where fuller teaching is needed.

checkQuestion: A child measured a rectangle and wrote its area as '63'. Another wrote a time as '15:45 pm'. Are these written with enough precision? Fix anything that isn't right, and say why the missing or wrong part matters.
checkAnswer: No single scored answer — listen for correcting '63' to '63 cm²' / '63 square centimetres' (area is measured in square units because it counts unit squares, not a bare number or a length unit) and recognising '15:45 pm' is wrong because 24-hour time uses no am/pm — it is 15:45, the same as 3:45 pm — and for saying why (63 alone doesn't say how much or of what; 15:45 pm mixes two systems). Surfaced for discussion, not scored.
